title: Vertex Cover approximation below factor two
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded finite simple undirected graph \(G\) of input bit length \(L\), the algorithm halts within \(B(L+1)^k\) Turing-machine steps and returns a vertex cover \(S\) satisfying
\[|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G),\qquad
\tau(G)=\min\{|T|:T\subseteq V(G),\ T\text{ is a vertex cover of }G\}?\]
The same positive improvement \(\varepsilon\) and the same algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no structural promise. Vertices have unit cost. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm-existence theorem or its unconditional negation.
definitions:
Graphs and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\ u\ne v\}\). For \(n=0\), the vertex set and edge set are empty. Edges are unordered pairs, with no loops or multiplicities. A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a vertex cover if every \(\{u,v\}\in E\) has \(u\in S\) or \(v\in S\). The quantity \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum cardinality of such a set; the minimum exists because the finite set \(V\) itself covers every edge. All vertices have weight one, so the cost is the number selected. If \(E=\varnothing\), then \(\tau(G)=0\), and the approximation inequality requires the output \(S=\varnothing\). Isolated vertices are allowed. The class includes disconnected, bipartite, nonbipartite, sparse and dense graphs without imposing any of those promises.

Input and output. The input is the full \(n\)-by-\(n\) binary adjacency matrix, preceded by a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\). One fixed encoding is \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(n+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(n+1)\rfloor+1\), followed by the matrix entries in row order. A valid input has a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal, and entry \((u,v)\) equals one exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). Its bit length is \(L=n^2+2b+1\). This explicitly includes all vertices, including isolated ones; there is no succinct matrix generator or graph oracle. The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector, with entry one exactly at selected vertices. Reading the input and writing this output count toward time. No guarantee is required on malformed encodings. Every labeling of the vertices by \([n]\) is a valid input order on which the guarantees must hold.

Computation. The algorithm is one deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes. Each step reads and writes one symbol on each tape, changes finite control and moves each head by at most one position. Work tapes are initially blank. No randomness, oracle, nonuniform advice or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. Integer or rational arithmetic, if used internally, is performed on finite binary representations with all bit operations charged. The time bound is worst-case over every valid input, rather than expected or amortized time. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once with the algorithm, not supplied as a graph-dependent accuracy parameter.

Quantifiers and accuracy. The order is
\[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists A\ \exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G.\]
The time constants may depend on this chosen algorithm and improvement but not on the input graph. Requiring a rational improvement does not change the original real-constant question: any positive real improvement implies a smaller positive rational one. The objective inequality is multiplicative, with no additive error, asymptotic slack or exceptional small graphs. A guarantee strictly below two separately on each finite graph, such as \(2-1/n\), does not give one improvement valid for all sizes. The numerical benchmark tolerance of 0.01 is not an additive tolerance on this approximation-ratio existence question.

context_blocks.text: A cover chooses vertices so that every edge is touched. A star with many leaves has optimum one, while a triangle has optimum two. The complement of a vertex cover is an independent set, but the identity between their optimum sizes does not preserve multiplicative approximation factors. This card uses unit vertex costs, retaining the unweighted target selected at admission.

The original seminar source discusses weighted Vertex Cover, its factor-two approximation, and its role in the primal-dual framework. The event was on 11 December 2000, and the online account is a summary by Claire Kenyon. It motivates the approximation barrier; it does not supply a contemporary status check or specify the full deterministic bit model used here.

Polynomial-time approximation bounds of the form \(2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\log n})\) improve on two at each sufficiently large fixed size. The improvement nevertheless tends to zero as \(n\) grows. Karakostas’s result therefore does not answer whether one fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) works on all inputs. The present deterministic target also requires the stated worst-case bit-time and output guarantees.

The 2-to-2 Games line of work proves NP-hardness of approximation within \(\sqrt2-\eta\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\). The 2025 Khot–Minzer–Safra journal account explains how later work proved the combinatorial hypotheses in its original reduction. This hardness gives an algorithmic impossibility consequence under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), but leaves a gap up to two and does not unconditionally rule out the algorithms quantified here.

Khot and Regev prove NP-hardness below every fixed factor \(2-\varepsilon\), assuming the Unique Games Conjecture. Thus UGC together with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would imply a negative answer to this card. Conversely, a deterministic improvement would contradict that conjunction; it would not by itself unconditionally refute UGC. If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), an exact polynomial-time cover algorithm would give a positive answer.

Claimed improvements require version and quantifier checks. The latest Salvador preprint, version 3 posted 6 July 2026, labels its universal \(7/4\) ratio as Conjecture 1, supported by finite experiments. The earlier version’s asserted \(7/5\) theorem is not the current conclusion. The latest version therefore supplies no proved fixed improvement for every graph.

The inspected March 2026 Hallelujah preprint states \(|S|<2\tau(G)\) for each finite nonempty graph, not a graph-independent positive gap. Its explicit lexicographic selection rule also has a direct limiting example: on \(K_{r,r}\) with the two parts labeled by alternating odd and even numbers, all degrees tie and the selected union has \(2r-1\) vertices while the optimum is \(r\). Its ratio is therefore \(2-1/r\). This observation concerns that preprint’s stated rule; the separately published version was accessible only through its abstract. Neither this pointwise claim nor its stated UGC interpretation certifies the target here.

The 6 September 2026 Karthik–Minzer preprint reports stronger NP-hardness for vertex cover in hypergraphs: factor \(1+\sqrt2-\eta\) for three-element edges, and \(k-\eta\) for fixed edge size \(k\ge4\). Ordinary graphs have two-element edges and are outside those new parameter ranges. The recent perfect-completeness four-to-one-games result likewise continues to list \(\sqrt2\) as the graph Vertex Cover hardness frontier in its introduction.

why: Vertex Cover is a basic covering problem with a long-standing gap between its factor-two algorithmic benchmark and known unconditional hardness thresholds. A fixed improvement would distinguish the true computational limit from a barrier shared by many methods. Ruling out every such algorithm would require an unconditional complexity separation, so the logical strength of the chosen question must remain explicit.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the formal statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), one deterministic program and common polynomial time constants, and prove termination, valid-cover output and \(|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\) on every valid adjacency-matrix input, including empty and edgeless graphs. A negative answer must prove that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every deterministic program having a polynomial running-time bound on all valid inputs, some graph produces an invalid cover encoding, an uncovered edge, or a cover larger than \((2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\). It must rule out all such algorithms, not merely one rounding scheme or restricted family. A conditional result under UGC, \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), ETH or another unproved hypothesis does not establish this unconditional negation. A vanishing improvement, experiments, an estimate of the optimum without a cover, or an algorithm restricted to a graph class does not meet the stated universal guarantee.

progress.text: Vazirani’s seminar discusses the factor-two approximation benchmark for weighted Vertex Cover; the retained card asks about unit weights.
Karakostas obtains the size-dependent ratio \(2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\log n})\), which tends to two rather than giving a fixed improvement.
Khot–Regev publish Unique-Games-based hardness below every fixed factor two; excluding polynomial algorithms additionally uses \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
The completed 2-to-2 Games proof sequence yields \(\sqrt2-\eta\) NP-hardness. Its role in the Vertex Cover reduction is documented in the 2025 journal account.
Salvador version 3 presents its \(7/4\) approximation ratio as a conjecture, not the proof of a uniform improvement claimed in an earlier version.
Karthik–Minzer report improved hardness for hyperedges of size three or at least four. Those ranges do not settle the graph case.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected established sources leave the fixed deterministic improvement open. Recent hypergraph hardness excludes the graph parameter k=2. Salvador version 3 explicitly leaves its 7/4 ratio conjectural; earlier version-2 claims do not represent its current result. The inspected Hallelujah preprint states a pointwise strict ratio, and its specified selection rule has ratios 2-1/r on alternating-labeled complete bipartite graphs, so it does not supply a fixed improvement. Full journal text of that work was unavailable. No matching resolution was found in the bounded source search; external proofs were not independently certified.

source_formulation.source: The 11 December 2000 Vazirani seminar summary provides the weighted factor-two motivation; Khot–Regev introduction and Khot–Minzer–Safra §1.1 explicitly discuss the fixed-improvement question.
source_formulation.interpretation: Preserved the admitted unweighted, general-graph, deterministic polynomial-time existence target. Rational epsilon is equivalent to the original existential real epsilon, and the adjacency-matrix bit encoding fixes implementation semantics. The target is unconditional algorithm existence, not merely UGC-based hardness or a claim about a particular heuristic.

sentences: A vertex cover selects at least one endpoint of every edge of a finite simple undirected graph.
The problem asks whether one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm always finds a cover within a fixed factor strictly below two of the minimum size.
The positive improvement must be independent of graph size, and the output and worst-case bit-time guarantees apply to every explicitly listed graph, including edgeless ones.
A complete Lean proof must establish such an algorithm or unconditionally rule out every polynomial-time candidate, rather than assume an unproved hardness hypothesis.
Known vanishing improvements, Unique-Games-based hardness, recent hypergraph results and the checked heuristic claims do not provide the required unconditional fixed-gap resolution.
